title: North Carolina mountain town ‘whitewashing’ violence amid crime concerns, says pastor with former gang ties
description: Dr. Ronald Gates says Asheville, North Carolina, leaders ignored his gang prevention program for a decade before retaliatory shootings rattled the city.
fullText:
An Asheville pastor who says he had gang ties as a young man told Fox News Digital that city leaders ignored his decade-long push for a youth gang-prevention program before recent violence rattled the North Carolina tourist city.

Dr. Ronald Gates first brought the proposal to Asheville officials in 2016, urging them to invest in early intervention for children he believes could otherwise be pulled into dangerous groups and retaliatory violence.

The issue has taken on new urgency after a string of retaliatory shootings left two people dead and seven others wounded. City officials have stopped short of calling the violence gang-related, instead describing it as retaliation between groups of friends.

Mountain Getaway Rocked By 'Latest Chapter' Of Deadly Violence As Officials Avoid Gang Label In Tourist Town

Gates believes that distinction misses the larger problem.

"They did not want to actually acknowledge that it was gang activity," Gates told Fox News Digital. "They wanted to make sure that they tried to whitewash the narrative as they're saying that these are just retaliations between individuals."

Gates is the senior pastor of Greater Works Church of God in Christ. He also serves as a Buncombe County Sheriff's Office chaplain and describes himself as a community liaison who works with local law enforcement. His work in those roles has heightened his concern about young people drawn to violence by money, territory or a need for belonging.

His proposal centers on Gang Free, a Los Angeles-based program intended to help students in grades four through six understand how gangs recruit children and the consequences of becoming involved.

Raleigh Mayor Considers Youth Curfew Following Teen Takeover, Violent July 4Th Weekend

Gates learned about the program during a 2016 trip to California and returned determined to bring a similar effort to Asheville before youth violence became more entrenched.

"I said, 'Man, I've got to bring this back to Asheville, North Carolina,'" he recalled.

Over the past decade, Gates said, he has presented the proposal to mayors, city and county managers, police chiefs and sheriff's officials, urging them to give it a one-year trial.

He questioned why the city had not invested in the program, even temporarily, to see whether it could work locally.

The program, Gates explained, would teach children how gangs operate, including their signs and colors, and explain how older members can use younger people to move drugs, carry weapons or carry out other crimes.

Police Bigwig Accused Of Driving Son's Getaway Car In Gang Shooing Is Sorority Sisters With Mayor: Report

But education alone is not enough, he argued. A prevention model must also provide young people an alternative to the money and status that can make gangs attractive.

"These young men want to help provide for their single mom or their family," Gates said. "Any money that they can hustle up, they feel like they're doing something or doing their part."

Under his proposal, law enforcement officers, mentors and local business owners would work directly with children in their neighborhoods. Along with gang-prevention lessons, the program would provide educational help, mentorship and exposure to entrepreneurship.

Local businesses could show students how they operate and offer a path to earning money legally, Gates said, while the city could help fund stipends or similar opportunities.

Chicago Mayor Warns Of 'Teen Trend' After Takeover Chaos, Violence Concerns Grow

"Now they're learning how to make honest money, business money, capital, instead of putting their life on the line," he said.

Gates also has personal reason to believe early intervention can matter.

Growing up in Grand Rapids, Michigan, Gates had gang ties and was loosely associated with the Vice Lords. He credited his father, older brother and sports with keeping him from becoming more deeply involved.

"I thank God that someone intervened," Gates said.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

That experience shaped his belief that prevention has to begin before children become immersed in street life. Young people without steady father figures or mentors can look to older gang members for guidance and protection, he said, creating an opening for those figures to pressure them into dangerous acts while avoiding the harshest consequences themselves.

"If they would have had the opportunity, a different path, a different choice … could they still be here today?" Gates said, referring to young people caught up in the recent violence.

Gates recalled being told in 2016 that Asheville did not have the kind of gang activity that would warrant the program. He warned at the time that city leaders needed to get ahead of the problem rather than wait for violence to escalate.

"I said, 'Give it two years,'" Gates said. "Two years to the year."

State data shows Asheville reported 42% more violent crimes in 2024 than in 2016, even as its overall crime index fell 8%. The increase was driven largely by aggravated assaults, which rose from 335 to 558, while reported robberies declined. Violent crime peaked in 2022 and fell for two consecutive years, though the 2024 total remained above the city's 2016 level.

Fox News Digital has contacted Asheville officials for comment on Gates' claim that he repeatedly presented the prevention program to city leaders beginning in 2016, whether the city reviewed it and why it was not adopted.

Gates stressed that he was not arguing every violent dispute in Asheville is gang-related. But he said the city should not wait for a formal gang label before acting when young people are caught in cycles of retaliation.

"You have personal disputes," Gates said. "But then the thrust behind it, the motivation behind it is because, 'Look here, you spilled some blood. I'm going to spill some blood also.' And that's what it has come to."

For city leaders, the question is not just how a crime is labeled, Gates argued, but whether young people have enough opportunities to avoid the path that can lead to prison or death.

That means practical support long before a shooting, arrest or funeral.

"The prevention, it works if you put it out there," he said.

His message to anyone considering retaliation is simple: Speak with an older relative, a business owner or another trusted adult before making a choice that could change or end a life.

"Is it even worth retaliating?" Gates said. "Is it worth losing my life or going to prison for the rest of my life?"

"Let's use common sense," he added. "Count up the real costs."

title: America’s Mediterranean lunch bowl is booming as NAYA races toward 200 restaurants

fullText:
When Hady Kfoury opened his first restaurant in Manhattan in 2008, he was already out of money. He had raised cash from friends and family to bring the Lebanese food he grew up eating to New York, but construction had cost more than he expected. He still owed money to his general contractor and resorted to buying equipment on eBay just to get the 54-seat restaurant open.

"It was a nightmare," Kfoury told Fortune.

The nightmare eventually turned into 48 restaurants and counting. NAYA now employs more than 1,000 people, with average annual sales of roughly $3 million per restaurant and same-store sales growth above 10% yearly. Its footprint has grown more than 40% in each of the past four years, just as Mediterranean bowls have become a fast-casual lunch staple. Kfoury's next target is 200 NAYAs by 2030.

Kfoury was born in Lebanon in 1981, during the country's civil war. He remembers some days going to school and other days having to take shelter in basements as bombs fell nearby. After studying hospitality in Switzerland and working in New York with chef Daniel Boulud, Kfoury returned to Lebanon, only to live through another war in 2006.

"I'm like, all right, that's not going to work," he recalled. "I have to move to the U.S., start a restaurant, and take the flavors that I was raised on and do it over there."

Kfoury had no track record as a restaurant owner, and after months of searching Midtown and Wall Street, he took a space on East 56th Street and Second Avenue. It happened to sit across the street from the aunt he'd stayed with during childhood trips to New York. The location wasn't busy enough for the high-volume concept he envisioned, so Kfoury opened NAYA as a fine-dining Lebanese restaurant instead.

His mother and aunt became what he calls the "culinary mastermind" behind it. His mother was a talented cook who didn't measure ingredients, so Kfoury convinced her to turn the food he had grown up eating—chicken kebabs, falafel, rice with vermicelli, baba ghanoush and hummus—into written recipes.

The restaurant attracted attention, but Kfoury hadn't abandoned his original idea. In 2010, he finally shifted NAYA to fast casual. The challenge was figuring out how to reproduce his family's food quickly and cheaply enough to serve hundreds of customers without stripping away what made it Lebanese.

title: US Treasury blocks certain journalists from G20 meeting in North Carolina
description: The U.S. Treasury Department is preventing certain journalists from covering a finance meeting among the world's most powerful countries, the latest example of how President Donald Trump's administrat...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Treasury Department is preventing certain journalists from covering a finance meeting among the world's most powerful countries, the latest example of how President Donald Trump's administration has restricted media access.

Individual reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg News were not granted credentials to the Group of 20 finance ministers' meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, the Times reported.

The Treasury has not explained the decision. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told The Associated Press in an interview Sunday that "it has nothing to do with point of view."

The reporters who've been denied access include the Times' Alan Rappeport, who has been covering such meetings and the Treasury Department since 2017. However, another reporter for the Times, Berlin bureau chief Jim Tankersley, is allowed to attend.

The Times said in a statement that denying American journalists access to an event in the U.S. is "not just another disturbing effort by the administration to undermine independent journalism, but a blatant attempt to evade public scrutiny."

"With the war in Iran, sanctions, the bond markets, and inflation on the agenda for the G20 finance ministers, the stakes of this gathering are significant for the global economy and the American people," the Times said. "Excluding specific reporters and entire news organizations is a disservice to the public and an assault on press freedoms that we strongly condemn."

Bloomberg News, in a story published Sunday evening, said "numerous" journalists from the news agency, including some based in Europe and Asia, had their accreditation requests rejected. It said denying the agency access to the meeting "undermines media freedom and public accountability."

The Wall Street Journal declined to comment.

Bessent is hosting the G20 meeting, which runs Saturday through Tuesday. It includes finance ministers, central bank governors and senior officials from the world's top economies. This year's G20 summit, which involves heads of state, is being held in December at Trump's golf club in Doral, Florida.

Tensions have been escalating between the U.S. media and the second Trump administration, playing out both in the public arena and at times in the courts.

For example, the Defense Department declared earlier this year that its press office had become a classified space inaccessible to journalists. The ouster came after the Pentagon had demanded that reporters agree to government-imposed restrictions on their work, prompting most news outlets to leave the building last fall.

The Associated Press has also sued Trump over access to the White House press pool. The news organization's access was curtailed for sticking with the name "Gulf of Mexico" after the administration ordered it rechristened the "Gulf of America."

title: Markey trounces Moulton in Massachusetts Senate primary poll

fullText:
Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) is handily leading Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.) in a primary race for his seat in the upper chamber, according to a new poll.

In the Emerson College Polling survey released Sunday, 60.4 percent of respondents — comprised of likely voters and those who have already voted — said they would back Markey if the primary were that day, while 32.8 percent said they would back Moulton and 6.7 percent were undecided.

Earlier this month, Moulton and Markey battled it out during the final Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary debate. The House member is running a long-shot campaign to oust the incumbent progressive senator in the primary this Tuesday.

Moulton, 47, has centered the race around generational change and questioned the progressive bona fides of Markey, 80. The representative has suggested the senator hasn't done enough to battle the Trump administration and push priorities such as the Green New Deal.

Markey, meanwhile, has noted his central role in writing the Green New Deal. He has also tried to tie Moulton to past votes and statements on issues like the Iran war and transgender rights.

Polling has often leaned in Markey's favor. The winner of the primary will likely take the Senate seat in the fall.

The Boston Globe announced that it was endorsing Moulton against Markey in recent weeks. The editorial board for the paper said Moulton "is promising that he can bring new vision and vigor to an aging, ailing, and deeply unpopular Democratic Party."

"It is true that Markey still looks and sounds sharp, and that he brings much valuable experience to the table," the board wrote. "But this is no ordinary time."

The Emerson College poll took place from Aug. 28-29, featuring 550 respondents and a credibility interval of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points.

title: Decontamination ongoing after MIT student reports creating dimethyl mercury
description: The school said the graduate student showed no signs of mercury exposure in an initial blood test but was under medical supervision as of Aug. 29.
fullText:
A Massachusetts Institute of Technology building was expected to remain closed at least through Aug. 30 after a graduate student was said to have created an unauthorized, highly toxic chemical compound.

The school's Aug. 29 statement said the student, who was not publicly identified, self-reported to an emergency room and said they had synthesized dimethyl mercury on Aug. 26. Less than 0.1 milliliters of the compound is a "severely toxic dose," according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

Dartmouth College professor Karen Wetterhahn died in 1997 after spilling "a few drops" of dimethyl mercury on her glove, according to the New Hampshire school. She developed health problems months after the spill that were discovered to be effects of acute mercury poisoning.

The MIT student showed no sign of mercury exposure in an initial blood test, the school said. The Aug. 29 statement also said updated information "calls into question" whether dimethyl mercury was synthesized.

The school said the student was under medical supervision and that Building 18 remained closed as "specialized decontamination efforts continue out of an abundance of caution."

High-touch surfaces in common areas of the student's residence hall were professionally cleaned, and decontamination of their individual unit was ongoing, MIT said. No restrictions were placed on the building.

Individuals who were near the student and affected workspace on Aug. 26 were offered baseline testing. Officials believe there is "very low risk of secondary or tertiary exposures" and do not recommend testing for individuals who were not in the student's lab space that day, the school said.

description: NICOSIA, Aug 30 () - At least eight people died and 18 were missing after a ferry carrying around 270 passengers and crew capsized off North Cyprus on Sunday, leaving survivors clinging to its overtur...
fullText:
NICOSIA, Aug 30 (Reuters) - At least eight people died and 18 were missing after a ferry carrying around 270 passengers and crew capsized off North Cyprus on Sunday, leaving survivors clinging to its overturned hull.

The privately owned ferry left the ‌port of Kyrenia at 12:30 p.m. local time (0930 GMT) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, authorities ‌said. It was heading for the Turkish port of Tasucu in the eastern Mediterranean.

Survivors reported the ferry moving erratically, with its last hard impact with the water's surface breaking ​the bow of the two-hulled vessel, allowing water to seep in. The boat was carrying 267 people, including a crew of eight, while 241 people were rescued.

The disaster occurred just off the coast of Kyrenia, a popular holiday resort for both locals and tourists. The ferry was one of several shuttle sea services that link North Cyprus, a breakaway unrecognised Turkish Cypriot state, with Turkey daily.

The incident has sent shockwaves through the territory. Hours after ‌the incident relatives remained outside a local hospital ⁠and the port gates in Kyrenia, waiting for news of their loved ones. Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman said he was "deeply saddened" by the incident.

Video footage showed people in red life jackets sitting or standing on top ⁠of the overturned vessel as authorities scrambled coastguard and private vessels for assistance to bring them to shore.

"The vessel had been moving very badly. It was constantly lifting out of the water and slamming back down. It was shaking violently," survivor Efe Multici told CNN Turk.

"Three or four minutes later, the ferry ​leapt ​high into the air, then came crashing down. The front left side burst ​open and water started pouring in."

Turkish Cypriot authorities said the ‌captain of the vessel and seven crew had been detained for questioning. By late afternoon, the ship had sunk, settling on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres (1,686 ft). Divers from Turkey would be assisting the search, they said.

"Search and rescue efforts will continue until the very end, until all people are reached," Erhurman told journalists after a crisis management meeting.

Cyprus was battered by fierce storms on Saturday, with one person dying after his sailboat crashed onto rocks in rough seas in the island's south-east.

Asked about the cause of the capsize, Erhurman ‌noted the storm on Saturday, but said the weather on Sunday was considered ​suitable for travel.

"There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something ​we have experienced before," he said.

North Cyprus is a breakaway state ​recognised only by Turkey, which supports the area economically and militarily.

In Turkey, President Tayyip Erdogan extended his condolences ‌to the families affected. Expressions of condolence and offers of ​assistance also came from Cyprus's internationally ​recognised government. Cyprus has been split down Greek and Turkish Cypriot lines since 1974, when Turkey invaded in response to a brief Greek-inspired coup.

"Efforts to reach those who are still missing continue uninterrupted," Erdogan said. "God willing, we hope to receive positive news from ​these efforts."

The Turkish Cypriot Interior Ministry said the ‌passenger ferry "FILOJET" was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew.

Four Turkish Cypriot coast guard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were ​deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, the ministry statement said.

title: Donald comes out of retirement to rejoin Rams
description: Aaron Donald, one of the NFL's greatest defensive players, has come out of retirement to rejoin his former side Los Angeles Rams.
fullText:
Aaron Donald, one of the NFL's greatest defensive players, has come out of retirement to rejoin his former side Los Angeles Rams.

The 35-year-old announced his immediate retirement in March 2024 after spending 10 seasons in the NFL, all with the Rams.

Donald, who was the 13th overall pick by the Rams in the 2014 draft, will rejoin on a reported one-year deal worth $20m., external

"We back," he posted on social media, with a video of his career highlights.

He helped the Rams win the Super Bowl in 2022 and is one of three men to be named the NFL's Defensive Player of the Year three times.

Donald finished his career with 117 sacks, two of them coming in the Rams' Super Bowl win.

He became the fastest defensive tackle to reach 100 sacks in NFL history and was an eight-time All-Pro selection.

title: 'I'll be back' - Itauma responds to world-title defeat
description: Great Britain's Moses Itauma says he will "be back" after failing in his attempt to become the second-youngest heavyweight world champion.
fullText:
Moses Itauma vowed "I'll be back" after failing in his attempt to become the second-youngest ever heavyweight world champion on Saturday.

Britain's Itauma, 21, tore through his first 14 opponents but his team threw in the towel in the ninth round against Filip Hrgovic at O2 Arena, London.

Having appeared to punch himself out, Itauma was barely able to stand as Hrgovic, 34, applied pressure to end the fight.

"It wasn't my night, we attempted greatness and just fell short to the more experienced man," Itauma said on social media.

"I want to say congratulations to Filip Hrgovic on his win. And although I never reached my desired outcome, I believe I gained experience that I'll take to my future fights.

"God bless, take care and I'll be back."

Heavyweight Itauma handed harsh world-title lesson

The vacant IBF title was on the line and Itauma was the favourite heading into the fight.

Hrgovic - who has lost only one professional fight, to Daniel Dubois in 2024 - is known for his durability, but he struggled to keep pace with Itauma early on.

However, his experience eventually told as the Briton was forced to leave the arena on a stretcher.

He was then taken to hospital and released overnight after having precautionary medical checks.

Queensberry Promotions boss Frank Warren believes Itauma needs a tactical rethink if he is to reach the top.

"That aura of invincibility, at the moment, is gone," Warren said. "People will look at that and maybe it will make it easier to make fights for him.

"He's still one of the most unbelievable talents I've ever been involved with. We'll stick with him. He needs a bit more ring craft and needs to stop thinking about knocking everyone out."

title: World number one Scheffler claims second Fedex Cup title
description: At times it felt like there was a certain inevitability about Scottie Scheffler collecting his second Fedex Cup title on Sunday.
fullText:
Tour Championship, final leaderboard

-16 S Scheffler (US); -13 V Hovland (Nor); -12 R Gerard (US); -11 A Fitzpatrick (Eng), C Gotterup (US), R McIlroy (NI), R Henley (US), MW Lee (Aus), J Bridgeman (US), L Aberg (Swe)

Selected others: -10 T Fleetwood (Eng), C Young (US), A Scott (Aus); -9 C Morikawa (US); -7 J Rose (Eng); -5 M Fitzpatrick (Eng), W Clark (US); E R MacIntyre (Sco)

At times it felt like there was a certain inevitability about Scottie Scheffler collecting his second Fedex Cup title on Sunday.

As those around him began to falter, the world number one, who started the day three strokes adrift of overnight leader Viktor Hovland, produced a typically metronomic performance with the winning cheque in sight.

And what a prize. Scheffler's reward for his 22nd career victory at the PGA Tour's season-ending Tour Championship in Atlanta will see his bank account credited to the tune of $10m (£7.4m).

It moves Scheffler to the top of the PGA Tour's career money list on $130.4m, above Tiger Woods, who has earned $120.9m and led the standings for the past 25 years.

The 2024 champion also joins Woods (2007 and 2009) and Rory McIlroy (2016, 2019 and 2022) as the only players to have won the event on multiple occasions.

"To come from behind and be able to win tournament is a really cool feeling," Scheffler said.

"There were a lot of talented guys in front of me on the leaderboard. I was fortunate to get off to a good start and put myself in the mix. It's a gift to be out here on tour. Each and every day I'm going to try to give it my best."

Across the final three pairings, Scheffler's four-under 66 was the only round to break par with his superb ability to find green after green giving him a substantial edge over his rivals.

Hovland, whose driving became more erratic, also found that his putter had gone cold when he most needed it, and the Norwegian signed for a two-over 72 as he finished three back in second place.

American debutant Ryan Gerard, who started one behind Hovland, ended the day in the same position and third overall on 12 under par after also taking 72 shots.

McIlroy was unable to rediscover the rhythm that rocketed him into contention on Saturday, with his topsy-turvy round of 69 containing four birdies, an eagle and five bogeys.

Aside from the Northern Irishman there were few moments of sparkle on show elsewhere among the potential contenders, albeit Justin Rose's slam-dunk hole-in-one on the par-three ninth was an obvious exception.

While Rose was unable to gather any momentum from that to seriously challenge, ending the day at seven under overall, another Englishman Alex Fitzpatrick matched Scheffler's 66, the lowest round of the day, to catapult himself up the leaderboard to conclude the tournament alongside six-time major winner McIlroy and five others at 11 under.

It earned the 27-year-old a tie for fourth on his debut to cap a remarkable season in which he won his first DP World Tour event at the Indian Open before teaming up with his elder brother, the 2022 US Open champion Matt, to win the Zurich Classic of New Orleans pairs event.

Tommy Fleetwood, who famously triumphed 12 months ago began the day too far off the pace for his three-under 67, to trouble the likes of Scheffler and ended in a tie for 11th at 10 under overall.

title: GB's Samuel earns first win at a Grand Slam - but 'nervous' Norrie beaten
description: British qualifier Toby Samuel breaks more new ground with a dominant victory over Tomas Machac on his US Open debut.
fullText:
British qualifier Toby Samuel broke more new ground with a dominant victory over Tomas Machac on his US Open main-draw debut.

The 23-year-old came from a set down in each of his three qualifying matches in New York this week to guarantee a third Grand Slam appearance of the year.

However, he had no such issues against former world number 20 Machac, wrapping up a 6-2 6-3 6-2 victory in just over 90 minutes to register his first win at a Grand Slam.

"It means everything to me. It's what I dreamt of as a kid watching these big tournaments," Samuel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Being able to win my first Grand Slam match is unbelievable."

Just two years ago, Samuel fell to almost 2,000th in the world rankings as bone bruising in his right arm ruled him out of much of the 2024 season.

He now sits inside the top 100 in the live ATP rankings, along with earning $140,000 (£103,000) in prize money in the biggest payday of his career so far.

Samuel won 36 of 39 matches on the ATP Challenger Tour to return to the top 300 last year, but has reached new heights in 2026.

The Winchester native came through qualifying to make his Grand Slam debut at the French Open, having never previously contested a single match on the ATP Tour.

He continued that momentum with a run to the semi-finals at Eastbourne, a Wimbledon wildcard, and a third Challenger crown of the year on Winnipeg's hard courts.

Samuel's new ranking would secure automatic qualification for next January's Australian Open, completing the set of major appearances a year after making his top-250 debut.

He is joined in the second round in New York by compatriot Katie Boulter, who battled past American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee 6-4 3-6 6-0.

How to follow US Open on the BBC

Admitting to being starstruck in the locker room at Roland Garros by the likes of Alexander Zverev, Samuel is slowly adjusting to his new surroundings.

"I'm still a little bit but I'm definitely more comfortable being around those top guys because I could be playing them the next day," he said.

"I have to start thinking of them not as stars but people I can play against."

Clinical in the opening two sets against Machac, he dropped just five points across his nine service games, including three successive holds to love as part of a seven-game winning run.

Trailing 2-0 at the start of the third set, he recovered to win the next six games – including saving two break points – to set up a second-round meeting with Czech 18th seed Jiri Lehecka.

Like Arthur Fery, his 2019 Wimbledon boys' doubles partners who shot up the rankings following an unexpected run to this year's SW19 semi-finals, Samuel has benefitted from the American collegiate system.

The former junior world number 57 was encouraged by his parents to pursue a degree at the University of South Carolina, where he won an All American doubles title and adjusted to the "super lively" crowds.

Several of his Carolina team-mates were in attendance for his first-round win, with Samuel crediting their "fighting energy" with helping him "get the job done" against Machac.

However his parents - who watched him throughout qualifying - were supporting another of their tennis-playing children on his college journey.

"My brother's just started university in America so they flew out to help him settle in, and I think my dad will fly back out for the second round," Samuel added.

Cameron Norrie, the 29th seed, believes he was his own worst enemy as he lost to Frenchman Luca Van Assche in four sets.

The British number two twice recovered from losing serve, including being broken in the first game of the match, to clinch the first-set in a tie-break, but only won seven games across the next three sets.

Tellingly, his unforced-error count (49) was more than double his opponent's (21) as he suffered a third consecutive first-round exit at a Grand Slam.

"It was really tough," said Norrie. "I was pretty nervous and it showed in the beginning of the first set, and I did well to steal that first set.

"I could never really maintain a good level of energy and momentum. That was super frustrating and pretty surprising.

"I felt like I lost to myself today."

British number four Jacob Fearnley will have to finish his first-round match on Monday after play on the outdoor courts was called off because of rain at about 9pm local time.

Fearnley, who was knocked out in qualifying but given a reprieve as a lucky loser, is a break down at 4-3 in the first set against Spain's 65th-ranked Martin Landaluce.
